recent_posts.title: Robot Talk Episode 154 – Visual navigation in insects and robots, with Andrew Philippides
recent_posts.summary: Andrew Philippides, Professor of Biorobotics at the University of Sussex, discusses how the navigation and learning abilities of ants and bees can inspire novel AI and biorobotic algorithms. His research combines biological experiments with robotics, modelling, and machine learning to understand how intelligent behaviour emerges from the interaction of body, brain, and environment, with a focus on visual navigation.

recent_posts.title: Ultralightweight sonar plus AI lets tiny drones navigate like bats
recent_posts.summary: Researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute developed a bat-inspired ultrasound perception system for small drones that enables navigation in low-visibility environments like smoke, fog, and darkness. The system combines a physical acoustic shield (inspired by bat ear cartilage) to reduce propeller noise with a neural network called Saranga that recovers weak echo signals from noisy measurements. Operating at milliwatt-level power, the approach reduces power by 1,000x, weight by 10x, and cost by 100x compared to existing solutions. Target applications include search and rescue, cave exploration, and anti-poaching operations where cameras and lidar fail.

recent_posts.title: Gradient-based planning for world models at longer horizons
recent_posts.summary: GRASP is a new gradient-based planner designed to make long-horizon planning with learned world models more practical and robust. The core problems addressed are: exploding/vanishing gradients from backpropagation through time, non-greedy local minima at longer horizons, and adversarial robustness issues when optimizing through high-dimensional deep learning models. GRASP uses a collocation (lifted-state) formulation that parallelizes optimization across time, injects Gaussian noise into virtual state updates for exploration, and avoids brittle state-input gradients by using only action Jacobians. A periodic refinement phase keeps trajectories grounded. Benchmarks on Push-T tasks show GRASP achieves higher success rates and faster planning times than CEM, standard gradient descent, and LatCo across horizons from H=40 to H=80.

recent_posts.title: Robot Talk Episode 153 – Origami-inspired robots, with Chenying Liu
recent_posts.summary: A podcast episode featuring Chenying Liu, Junior Research Fellow at the University of Oxford, discussing origami-inspired robots and embodied physical intelligence. The conversation covers how a robot's physical form — through geometry, materials, and control — can actively contribute to sensing, processing, decision-making, and movement, enabling more autonomous and resilient robotic systems.

recent_posts.title: Sony AI table tennis robot outplays elite human players
recent_posts.summary: Sony AI has published research in Nature introducing Ace, a robot that becomes the first to defeat elite human players in a competitive physical sport. Ace combines event-based vision sensors with model-free reinforcement learning and high-speed hardware. In official matches under ITTF regulations, Ace won three of five matches against elite players and later beat professional players in follow-up matches. The robot achieved over 75% return rate on spins up to 450 rad/s and demonstrated the ability to generalize to rare, hard-to-simulate situations like balls bouncing off the net.

recent_posts.title: AI system learns to keep warehouse robot traffic running smoothly
recent_posts.summary: MIT and Symbotic researchers developed a hybrid AI system that uses deep reinforcement learning combined with classical planning algorithms to coordinate hundreds of robots in e-commerce warehouses. The system learns which robots to prioritize at each moment to prevent congestion, achieving roughly 25% greater throughput than traditional expert-designed algorithms in simulations. The approach adapts to different warehouse layouts and robot densities, and scales better than conventional methods as robot density increases. Real-world deployment is still a future goal, with plans to extend the system to task assignment and larger fleets.

recent_posts.title: Robot Talk Episode 152 – Dexterous robot hands, with Rich Walker
recent_posts.summary: Rich Walker from Shadow Robot Company discusses dexterous robotic hands developed for research and industrial applications. Walker, a long-time Shadow Robot veteran who moved from software and systems engineering into management, covers the company's R&D initiatives across the UK and Europe, proof-of-concept projects for dexterous robotics, and his role representing robotics SMEs through euRobotics.

recent_posts.title: What I’ve learned from 25 years of automated science, and what the future holds: an interview with Ross King
recent_posts.summary: Ross King, creator of Adam — the first robot scientist — reflects on 25 years of automated science research. He discusses how AI has transformed scientific discovery, the limitations of current LLMs for autonomous research, and the Nobel Turing Challenge aiming to build an AI capable of Nobel-level science by 2050. King also explains his work on DNA computing, which leverages biology's self-replication to achieve exponentially denser compute than electronics, and his current Genesis project using bioreactors to study yeast metabolism as a stepping stone to understanding human cells. He argues that AI plus human scientists already outperforms humans alone, and that the economics of science are shifting as automation reduces costs.

recent_posts.title: Generative AI improves a wireless vision system that sees through obstructions
recent_posts.summary: MIT researchers developed two systems that use generative AI to improve wireless vision through obstructions. The first, Wave-Former, uses millimeter wave (mmWave) signals to partially reconstruct hidden 3D objects, then employs a specially trained generative AI model to fill in missing geometry caused by specular reflections — achieving ~20% accuracy improvement over baselines. The second system, RISE, reconstructs entire indoor scenes using multipath mmWave reflections off moving humans from a single stationary radar, producing reconstructions twice as precise as existing methods. A key innovation was adapting large computer vision datasets to simulate mmWave reflection physics, bypassing the lack of large mmWave training datasets. Applications include warehouse robots verifying packed items and smart home robots tracking human location while preserving privacy.

recent_posts.title: Resource-constrained image generation and visual understanding: an interview with Aniket Roy
recent_posts.summary: Aniket Roy, a recent Johns Hopkins PhD graduate now at NEC Laboratories America, discusses his research on resource-constrained image generation and visual understanding. His work spans few-shot learning (FeLMi), caption-guided augmentation (Cap2Aug), perceptual quality improvement in diffusion models via kurtosis concentration loss (DiffNat), and parameter-efficient personalization using LoRA-based frameworks (DuoLoRA, MultiLFG). A key insight is that classical image statistics — specifically kurtosis consistency across wavelet frequency bands — can improve perceptual realism in modern diffusion models without full retraining. His research targets making large generative models more efficient and adaptable under data and compute constraints.
